source.title: Demystifying optimized prompts in language models
source.authors: Rimon Melamed; Lucas H. McCabe; H. H. Huang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies optimized prompts and their activation patterns, but does not test superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE feature recovery, or one-dimensional feature geometry as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports sparse-probe and feature-ablation results on optimized versus natural-language prompts; these are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the listed versions. Token influence and frequency analyses, and layer-wise KL trajectories, do not measure the claim's feature geometry and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes GCG-optimized prompts (token composition, sparse probes on neuron activations, ablation of top mean-difference dimensions, logit-lens KL). It does not measure superposition, polysemanticity, SAE feature recovery, or feature dimensionality; sparse probing here detects prompt type, not features spread across neurons. It neither tests nor relies on the superposition claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Optimized prompts mainly use punctuation and nouns that are rarer in training data. Sparse probes separate them from natural prompts. Ablating top neurons does not hurt them more than natural prompts. Instruction-tuned models show a similar layer-wise KL trajectory.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GCG within the evil-twins prompt-optimization framework and analyzes prompt tokens and model activations; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report stronger ablation effects in the first and final layers for some models; most layers show no large difference between optimized and natural-language prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse neuron-level probes separate optimized from natural prompts with high accuracy, but ablating the top-ranked neurons hurts both prompt types similarly in most layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized prompts have sparse, linearly separable activation signatures that do not imply greater reliance on those dimensions.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Results for the probe and ablation experiments are described qualitatively in the text, while exact plotted values are not stated there; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors limit analysis to models up to 8 billion parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Token-composition and token-frequency results do not measure the claim's feature geometry. Layer-wise KL trajectories compare prompt representations in vocabulary space, not superposition or feature directions.

untested.parts: All: toy networks, sparsity-dependent transitions, geometry of overlapping directions.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
All: non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
All: distributed features across neurons or SAE-recoverable sparse features in LLMs (no SAEs used; neuron-level probes only for prompt type).
All: completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is unrelated to superposition beyond citing SAE work in related work. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse feature counts relative to dimensions, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Whether real-model features are spread across neurons or sparse semantic features are recoverable with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: tested models (aggregate statement)
rows.size_stated: models up to 8 billion parameters; individual sizes not stated for this aggregate result
rows.operation_detail: Trained sparse linear classifiers on top-ranked activation features to distinguish optimized prompts from their natural-language counterparts.

conditions.value: top-ranked features at each layer; varying sparsity

rows.baseline: Near-random accuracy for natural-language versus other natural-language prompts and natural-language versus random prompts
rows.value: High accuracy, including under high sparsity; exact values are figure-only
rows.note: The text reports an aggregate qualitative result across models; it does not establish recovery of semantic or SAE features.
rows.check: Probe accuracy distinguishing optimized from natural prompts measures prompt-type separability, not superposition or SAE feature recovery. State 'observed' refers to the study's own finding, not to any version; set to cannot_determine for the claim. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: tested models (aggregate statement)
rows.size_stated: models up to 8 billion parameters; individual sizes not stated for this aggregate result
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed top-ranked activation dimensions identified by mean difference, then measured top-10 token prediction overlap.

conditions.value: most layers; some models show stronger effects in first and final layers

rows.measure: Top-10 token prediction overlap after feature ablation
rows.value: Top-feature ablations affect both prompt types compared with random-feature ablations; for most layers in each model, effects on optimized prompts are not substantially different from effects on natural-language prompts. Exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The paper's prose describes the qualitative findings, but this measure does not determine whether features are superposed or have the geometry in the claim.
rows.check: Ablation of top mean-difference neurons measures reliance on those dimensions, not feature geometry or superposition. The link of none and the state are correct.
